summary:
Stavropol Krai stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been banned outright since 2023. The expanded "propaganda" statute criminalises public expression that, explicitly, justifies gender transition, and the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation. Foreign nationals who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days, and deportation. The US State Department carries a Level 4, Do Not Travel advisory for Russia with warnings directed at LGBT travellers, and Global Affairs Canada advises avoiding all travel to the country.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) identifies the North Caucasus as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory assessment of Russia. Within this zone, trans people and public LGBT+ advocates are assessed as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, with systematic regional campaigns recorded across 2017 to 2024. Charges following the 2023 extremist designation carry two to six years' imprisonment, rising to six to ten years for organising.

Movement into the neighbouring North Caucasus entities is restricted for visitors: Global Affairs Canada reports that Ministry of Interior special permission is required to enter Kabardino-Balkaria, including the Elbrus area, Karachai-Cherkessia and North Ossetia. The same advisory records that 2SLGBTQI+ persons and the families of their allies have been attacked, harassed and abused, that advocacy organisations have been treated as extremist since January 2024, and that foreign visitors are subject to surveillance.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, speaking to the Human Rights House Foundation as a North Caucasus defender in exile, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the region and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. He reports a year-on-year deterioration in conditions.
tangentialFactors:
The UK Home Office's finding for Russia as a whole is that LGBT+ persecution is not established, which makes the North Caucasus carve-out the operative standard for anyone travelling to Stavropol Krai and its neighbouring territories. Applicants and visitors assessed against the national baseline may therefore understate the exposure recorded for this region.

Global Affairs Canada's advisory for Russia combines the LGBT-specific warnings with a general security environment in which terrorist attacks are recorded in Chechnya, Dagestan, Ingushetia and the Stavropol region. These conditions affect routing and transport planning across the area rather than indicating any trans-specific risk on their own.

Regional conditions are described as worsening rather than static. Isteev's assessment of continuous year-on-year deterioration aligns with the UK Home Office's documentation of sustained campaigns between 2017 and 2024 and with the national escalation in extremism charges after the 2023 designation.
localsOnly:
Residents of Stavropol Krai live under the same national prohibitions on legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care that apply across Russia, alongside the extremist designation and the propaganda provisions covering public expression that justifies gender transition.

For people living in the region, the UK Home Office documentation of systematic campaigns between 2017 and 2024 indicates sustained organised activity rather than isolated incidents. Extremism charges connected to the 2023 designation carry two to six years' imprisonment, and six to ten years for organising, while advocacy organisations have been treated as extremist since January 2024.

Isteev reports that private existence in the North Caucasus can itself trigger violence, detention or forced return to families, and that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people there. Reporting suggests some residents have sought safety by leaving the region, with defenders continuing to work from exile.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Stavropol Krai-specific court decisions, detentions or raids are recorded in the source inventory; the legal exposure described here derives from the national framework and from the UK Home Office's regional assessment of the North Caucasus, and direct local enforcement patterns remain unsourced.

The precise wording by which the UK Home Office names individual North Caucasus territories in its June 2025 note, including whether Stavropol Krai is listed separately from the republics and autonomies, is not verifiable from the inventory and is treated as unresolved here.

Frequency data for the terrorist attacks cited for the Stavropol region, and the practical procedure and processing times for Ministry of Interior special permission into the neighbouring territories, are not sourced.

Whether the families of LGBT travellers face specific risk under the documented pattern of attacks on allies' families is recorded by Global Affairs Canada in general terms, with no region-specific figures available.
